issues.legal_issue: A witness’s delayed disclosure cannot be treated as making the witness unreliable merely because the witness did not react or speak in a particular way when the circumstances provide an explanation.
material_facts: A young eyewitness testified that he saw the accused throttle the victim and that the accused threatened him.
The eyewitness did not disclose what he had seen for about three days.
The record did not support the finding that the eyewitness had first said he had not seen the occurrence or had refused cross-examination.
issues.conclusion: The delay and silence were not suspicious or unnatural in the circumstances, and the eyewitness’s testimony should not have been discarded on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Human reactions vary, and there is no fixed rule of natural reaction by which a witness’s evidence may be rejected. Discarding evidence because a witness did not react in a particular manner is unrealistic. The Court relied on Rana Partap and Ors. v. State of Haryana, 1983 (3) SCC 327; it cited no statutory provision for this principle.

rule.if: criminal_case_with_eyewitness_testimony and eyewitness_delayed_disclosure and witness_feared_accused and no_record_supporting_prior_denial

predicates.criminal_case_with_eyewitness_testimony: The proceeding is a criminal case in which a witness testified to seeing the offence.
predicates.eyewitness_delayed_disclosure: The eyewitness did not disclose what the eyewitness had seen until some time after the event.
predicates.witness_feared_accused: The eyewitness said the accused had threatened the eyewitness, explaining the delay in disclosure.
predicates.no_record_supporting_prior_denial: The record did not show that the eyewitness had earlier denied seeing the event.

issues.definition: When an eyewitness in a criminal case delays disclosure, feared the accused, and the record does not support a claimed prior denial, the delay does not by itself make the testimony unreliable.

issues.legal_issue: Evidence that the victim was last seen with the accused, combined with recovery of the victim’s body from the accused’s field and the accused’s initial prevention of a search, can establish the accused’s guilt.
material_facts: Witnesses testified that they saw the victim with the accused shortly before the occurrence.
The victim’s body was found buried in the accused’s field.
The accused initially prevented the victim’s father and others from searching the field, and later permitted the search after persuasion.
The eyewitness’s testimony that the accused throttled the victim also supported the prosecution case.
issues.conclusion: The last-seen evidence and the circumstances of the body’s recovery, particularly the accused’s initial resistance to the search, were sufficient in combination to substantiate guilt; the evidence as a whole established responsibility for the rape and murder.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the last-seen evidence together with the recovery of the body from the accused’s field and the accused’s initial resistance to the search as significant corroborating circumstances. It cited no statutory provision or earlier case for this conclusion.

predicates.criminal_prosecution: The proceeding is a criminal prosecution for an offence against the victim.
predicates.victim_seen_with_accused_shortly_before_: Witnesses saw the victim with the accused shortly before the offence occurred.
predicates.victim_body_found_in_accused_controlled_: The victim’s body was recovered from a place controlled by the accused.
predicates.accused_initially_prevented_search: The accused initially stopped others from searching the place where the victim’s body was later found.

issues.definition: In a criminal prosecution, when the victim was seen with the accused shortly before the offence, the body was found in a place controlled by the accused, and the accused initially prevented a search, those circumstances together can establish the accused’s guilt.

issues.legal_issue: An acquittal may be set aside on appeal when the conclusions supporting it are patently perverse.
material_facts: The trial court convicted the accused and imposed sentences for rape, murder, and causing disappearance of evidence.

The High Court reversed the conviction and acquitted the accused, including after rejecting the eyewitness evidence and failing to give due consideration to the last-seen evidence and other circumstances.
The Supreme Court found the High Court’s conclusions patently perverse.
issues.conclusion: The acquittal was indefensible and was set aside; the trial court’s conviction and sentences were restored.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the judgment of acquittal could not stand in light of the patently perverse conclusions reached by the appellate court. It cited no statutory provision or earlier case for this appellate ruling.

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a judgment of acquittal.
predicates.acquittal_based_on_patently_perverse_con: The acquittal rests on conclusions that are patently perverse.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an acquittal and the acquittal rests on patently perverse conclusions, the acquittal is set aside and the trial conviction is restored.
